Senator Anne Carney, Chair Representative Amy Kuhn, Chair Committee on Judiciary 100 State House Station, Room 438 Augusta, ME 04330
RE: LD 1650 - An Act to Allow Paralegals to Be Paid by the Maine Commission on Public Defense Services
Dear Senator Carney, Representative Kuhn, and Members of the Committee on Judiciary,
MACDL supports all efforts to better serve indigent defendants in Maine's criminal justice system - including employment of paralegals by the Maine Commission on Public Defense Services ("PDS"). There is no doubt that paralegals play a vital role in supporting quality legal representation. However, LD 1650 is not the best way to accomplish this objective, and therefore MACDL is neither for nor against LD 1650.
Paralegal standards and rates of compensation should be developed by the Maine Commission on Public Defense Services. PDS was created to oversee and improve our indigent defense system. PDS is better suited than the Legislature to evaluate the operational needs of public defenders and to implement a sustainable, responsive system for paralegal reimbursement - one that considers training, qualifications, case complexity, and fiscal oversight.
Currently, there is already a mechanism through PDS to compensate paralegals for their work on cases. Imposing rigid mandates from the Legislature could inadvertently hinder PDS's flexibility to address evolving needs and fiscal realities.
In short, MACDL urges you to support the mission behind LD 1650, but leave the implementation details to the expertise of the Maine Commission on Public Defense Services. This will ensure that we strengthen our public defense system thoughtfully and responsibly. For these reasons, MACDL is neither for nor against LD 1650.

Sincerely,

/s/ Eric S. Thistle Eric S. Thistle, Esq. MACDL Member
10045157:
GINA TURCOTTE SIDNEY LD 1650
My name is GinA Turcotte. I proposed and am testifying in support of LD #1650 An Act to Allow Paralegals to Be Paid by the Maine Commission on Public Defense Services.
As we try to find solutions to our current court crisis, I have heard very little about paralegals' ability to help resolve it. What exactly do the public defense attorneys need? At least one answer is: more help to do the work that is constitutionally required for each defendant. Who do attorneys typically depend on to help them? Paralegals.
I am a litigation paralegal and have worked in the legal industry for over 30 years, first as a legal secretary and then as a paralegal for the past several years for an attorney with 60yrs of practice. Working alongside and being mentored by seasoned attorneys has provided me with professional competence and skills comparable to those attorneys' skills.
I recently worked with Attorney Jennifer Cohen and was paid by the Commission under court order for a pro se criminal defendant. Upon reviewing the Commission's fee schedule at Ch. 301, Sec. 3(1), it allows for payment of fees and reimbursement for paralegal services through non-counsel cost procedures, but it does not expressly authorize public defense attorneys to hire paralegals at the Commission's expense. I believe the Commission's rules and our state laws need to expressly authorize, and perhaps even require, public defense attorneys to hire a minimum of 2 paralegals to assist with indigent clients' cases at the Commission's expense and set out a fee schedule for that paralegal work.
By allowing public defense attorneys to hire paralegals who are paid by the Commission, those paralegals can maintain contact with clients, communicate with other parties, and do the legal work that does not need to be done by the attorneys which will naturally increase the attorneys' productivity and legal effectiveness while their invoices will decrease. Given that the average labor market rate for paralegals in Maine, depending on region, is $30/hr, and public defenders are now receiving $150/hr, indigent clients will benefit from five times the amount of work by paralegals for the same cost as one hour of work by their public defender.
In closing, by enacting this bill into law, not only will it alleviate the financial burden on taxpayers, but it will also provide hundreds of good paying jobs for people who want to work as paralegals to provide indigent defendants with the legal defense they are entitled to receive. If this bill is scrutinized objectively, its enactment into law would create a win win situation for the courts, taxpayers, attorneys and indigent defendants and would most assuredly reduce the court docket at a faster speed. Thank you for your attention and allowing me to testify. I would be happy to answer any questions you may have.

Executive Director Jim Billings
To: Senator Anne Carney Representative Amy Kuhn Joint Standing Committee on Judiciary
From: Jim Billings, Executive Director, Maine Commission on Public Defense Services RE: LD 1650 "An Act to Allow Paralegals to Be Paid by the Maine Commission on Public Defense
Services" Date: April 23, 2025
The Maine Commission on Public Defense Services submits the following testimony in opposition to LD 1650.
LD 1650 seeks to compel PDS to implement a system to compensate paralegals employed to help provide indigent legal services at the average labor market rate for paralegal services.
PDS already has a system in place created via administrative rule to provide counsel with reimbursement for paralegal services used in assigned cases on a case-by-case basis. PDS is currently engaged in rulemaking to expand this program by making it easier for attorneys to access paralegal services.
The requirement that compensation be fixed to the "average labor market rate for paralegal services" is problematic. This bill offers no methodology for determining that rate. It is also silent whether that rate will be set on a statewide, county, or regional basis. This rule would also treat paralegals differently than all other noncounsel vendors used by assigned counsel whose services are not compensated at market rates. For example, private investigators are currently providing services on PDS cases at a reduced rate.
PDS conducted a survey in 2024 seeking data on market rates for attorney and paralegal services in retained matters. The results of that survey showed an average paralegal rate of $113 per hour. PDS has reason to believe that a true market rate would be even higher if PDS has to include all paralegals, including those employed by large civil litigation firms, some of which charge as much or even more than the current $150/hour rate paid to assigned counsel. The bill as currently drafted would have a significant effect on MCPDS's budget and would require significant research and analysis to come up with an accurate projection upon which to generate a fiscal note.
The bill also will have a negative effect on the participation of rostered attorneys and other vendors who are paid well below market rate. The bill sends a signal to counsel and investigators that their services are not valued enough to deserve their market rates while the services of paralegals are.
/s/ James A. Billings James A. Billings Executive Director MCPDS

Sen. Anne Carney, Chair Rep. Amy Kuhn, Chair Joint Standing Committee on Judiciary Maine State Legislature 100 State House Station Augusta, ME 04333
Re: LD 1650, An Act to Allow Paralegals to Be Paid by the Maine Commission on Public Defense Services
Dear Sen. Carney, Rep. Kuhn, and Members of the Judiciary Committee:
On behalf of the Board of Governors of the Maine State Bar Association, we write to provide comments in support of LD 1650, An Act to Allow Paralegals to Be Paid by the Maine Commission on Public Defense Services. The ability of the Maine Commission on Public Defense Services (Commission) to pay paralegal fees will increase efficiencies, reduce costs associated with representation of a given matter, and increase parity between defense attorneys and prosecutorial districts in terms of support staff. In expressing support for the bill as drafted, we understand there is a potential amendment that would replace the bill with a pilot project. We would be supportive of this approach as well if it represents the best opportunity to move forward with increased use of paralegals in indigent legal defense. Additionally, we understand the Commission has initiated administrative rulemaking to establish requirements and procedures for paying paralegals and legal secretaries who support appointed counsel. To the extent the Commission's rulemaking may achieve the goals of LD 1650, this legislation may not be necessary.
About MSBA. The Maine State Bar Association is a statewide trade association chartered in 1891 by the Maine Legislature. The Association currently represents approximately 2,500 attorneys in the State in both public service and private practice. The Association maintains 28 separate sections covering nearly every field of law practiced in Maine, from Administrative Law to Workers' Compensation Law.
What does LD 1650 do? LD 1650 directs the Commission to develop and maintain a system to compensate paralegals employed by defense attorneys who undertake court-appointed defense work. The bill specifies that payment for paralegals would be at the average labor market rate for paralegal services. The potential amendment to the bill would limit the scope of the bill to a one-year pilot project in the Kennebec County public defense office only.
Discussion. It is a standard practice across the legal industry for law firms to bill clients for paralegals' work on their matters, generally at a reduced hourly rate compared to the attorney handling the matter. To the extent the current system does not enable paralegals that work with attorneys who undertake courtappointed work to receive compensation from the Commission, it creates inefficiencies.
A smoother system for compensation of paralegals by the Commission could lead to important case efficiencies and cost savings. When an attorney works closely with a paralegal, the attorney can pass off certain tasks to the paralegal and free up their own time to take on other work. Employing paralegals would allow attorneys to take on additional court-appointed clients and ease the underrepresentation crisis facing the state. Moreover, because paralegals' time spent on matters would be billed at a lower hourly

rate, the overall cost of defense representation would go down, easing pressure on the Commission's strained budget.
Additionally, LD 1650 would increase parity between defense attorneys and prosecutorial districts with regard to support staff. District Attorneys' offices and the Office of the Attorney General's criminal division employ paralegals and administrative staff to assist prosecutors. The support staff are critical for the functioning of these offices and greatly increase the overall quality of representation afforded to the State. LD 1650 would represent an important step towards parity in terms of resources available for prosecution and defense in Maine.
Although we strongly support the goal of LD 1650 - compensation by the Commission for paralegal services - we do not mean to weigh in on whether the goal is best achieved through legislation or administrative rulemaking by the Commission. To the extent the rulemaking process on this topic initiated by the Commission earlier this spring accomplishes the goals of LD 1650, this legislation may not be necessary.
Conclusion. Thank you for the opportunity to provide this letter in support of LD 1650, which would increase efficiencies in the indigent criminal defense system and provide a step towards parity between prosecutors' offices and defense attorneys. If you have questions or need additional information, please do not hesitate to let us know.
Sincerely,
